Motion / Particle dome

Particle dome

The brand-signature ambient animation. A 15,000-particle (production) or 5,000-particle (this preview) point cloud arranged as a hemispherical dome that breathes — size oscillates with inverse-coupled per-vertex distortion, plus multi-axis rotation drifting between dominant axes. Renders to a WebGL canvas via Three.js (r128, dynamically loaded on first appearance, ~150 KB gzipped, cached after first load). Dark-only at v1 (additive blending of white particles depends on a dark backdrop). Respects prefers-reduced-motion: reduce — animation halts and the dome holds at the starting frame. Pauses when scrolled offscreen via IntersectionObserver to spare GPU.

Variants

Single variant at v1 — the breathing dome. Two presets: data-ds-particle-scale="preview" (5,000 points, smaller radius, for docs / contained surfaces) and data-ds-particle-scale="hero" (15,000 points, production scale, for marketing-site Hero composition Variant E).

on-dark · preview scale

Usage rules

Hero only. The dome is the focal-moment animation — use it behind a primary marketing-site hero and nowhere else. Dropping it into content sections, data viz, or below-the-fold folds dilutes its signal and burns GPU continuously for a decorative element the reader has scrolled past.

Production scale is 15,000 points. Use data-ds-particle-scale="hero" on marketing pages. The preview scale (5,000 points) is for docs / contained surfaces only — it captures the breathing motion at a fraction of the GPU cost so the docs site stays responsive when this page is open.

Dark backdrop is non-negotiable. The dome reads as light particles glowing through space — that requires THREE.AdditiveBlending against a dark surface. A light-variant dome would need a different blend mode, different particle color, and a different visual identity — not the same component. Deferred to v2 of this primitive.

Reduced-motion: hold first frame. Users who've set prefers-reduced-motion: reduce see the dome at its starting state (size = base + amplitude, all phases at 0) with no animation. The visual signature is preserved; the motion isn't.

Pauses when offscreen. IntersectionObserver halts the render loop when the dome's container scrolls out of view. Resumes on re-entry. This is the same pattern .ds-marquee uses for tickers — saves CPU + battery on long pages where the dome sits in the hero.

Fallback for failed WebGL load. If Three.js fails to fetch (offline / blocked CDN / browser without WebGL), the container falls back to a subtle radial-gradient glow so the surface doesn't render as a flat black void. The [data-ds-particle-failed] attribute on the container triggers the fallback CSS.

Decorative, never interactive. The container has pointer-events: none — the dome never blocks clicks on UI behind it. The canvas carries aria-hidden="true" — screen readers skip it entirely.

Composes inside templates, not standalone. The dome is a positioned-absolute decoration behind content. Real usage: drop <div class="ds-particle-dome" data-ds-particle-dome data-ds-particle-scale="hero"></div> as the first child of a .ds-hero with position: relative, set z-index: 0 on it and z-index: 1 on the content. See Hero composition Variant E — Animated for the full pattern.

Performance notes

Three.js bundle ≈ 150 KB gzipped. Dynamically loaded on first .ds-particle-dome appearance — pages without the dome pay 0 KB. After first load, browser caches the CDN bundle indefinitely.

Device-pixel-ratio capped at 2×. On Retina displays the renderer caps DPR at 2 instead of using the device's actual ratio (often 3×). Visual difference is negligible at this particle density; frame-rate gain is real.

15K points × ~60fps measures comfortably on mid-tier laptops and recent phones. Older devices (4-year-old Android, low-end Chromebooks) throttle — the IntersectionObserver pause is the main mitigation; reduced-motion is the user opt-out.

Previous← Motion atoms NextASCII →
Illustration / ASCII

ASCII

* What changed in v2.1 Canvas-clamp baked into the base rule: .ascii-illustration > canvas { width: 100% !important; height: 100% !important; object-fit: contain } + .ascii-illustration { overflow: hidden }. Was a consumer-side override before — every page using the illustration had to re-implement it. The renderer's intrinsic 1440px canvas no longer overflows. NEW background-watermark variant inside .ds-hero--split: on mobile the illustration auto-promotes to opacity 0.10 / 0.08 behind the copy block.

Source images rendered as animated ASCII illustrations — chunky pixel blocks resolving into binary digits on scroll-into-view. The metaphor mirrors what VideoDB does to a frame at runtime: pixels become the binary representation that agents read. JetBrains Mono throughout, near-white characters on dark, scroll-triggered, honours prefers-reduced-motion: reduce.

Example

The animation plays a multi-stage build-up — coarse 30-col blocks dissolve in one cell at a time, then snap through 60-col and 120-col grids, then morph cell-by-cell to binary digits. Per-cell timings are re-randomised on every replay, so the dissolve pattern is never the same twice.

Replay behaviour

Two modes, configurable via the data-replay attribute. Default is always — the animation replays every time the section enters the viewport. Switch to once for a one-shot intro that holds the binary state after the first play. Toggle below to see the live difference; press Replay now to trigger immediately.

Usage rules

Source image is a real file on disk. The renderer samples a preprocessed PNG via an offscreen canvas. The preprocessing step (composite onto white, auto-invert, edge flood-fill, autocrop, autocontrast, unsharp, posterise to 4 levels) lives in the ascii-converter skill — don't author with photographic images directly, let the skill preprocess first.

JetBrains Mono only. The character grid relies on monospace metrics. Other fonts will misalign the cells; the renderer waits for the JBM font to load before measuring cell width.

Dark backdrop is the default. Near-white characters (#F5F5F7) on near-black (#0A0A0A) is the canonical pairing. A light-surface variant would need a different colour treatment and isn't shipped at v1.

Per-cell timings re-randomise on every replay. The dissolve order isn't memorised — each playback's pattern is different, which keeps repeated views from feeling mechanical.

Reduced-motion: skip the animation. Users with prefers-reduced-motion: reduce see the final binary state immediately, with no morph or dissolve. The illustration is still legible; the motion isn't.

Pauses when offscreen. IntersectionObserver halts the animation as soon as the element leaves the viewport and re-triggers on re-entry (subject to the replay mode).

Performance notes

Three resolution levels precomputed at load. For a 120-col fine resolution that's ~8,400 fine cells + ~2,100 mid + ~525 coarse ≈ 11,000 cells total. Negligible memory; one canvas per illustration.

Animation runs at requestAnimationFrame. CPU spikes during the morph (full fine grid), settles to zero in the held-binary state. No render loop when idle.

Asset size depends on the source. Preprocessed PNGs land at ~50 KB for a 1024×1024 four-level image. The runtime itself is ~6 KB inlined in this page.

Motion / Components / Motion wrapper

Motion wrapper

The reusable wrapper for any pre-rendered MP4 motion organism. Composes a <video autoplay muted loop playsinline> with the system's autoplay contract, surface variants, reduced-motion gate, IntersectionObserver pause, and graceful fallback for failed loads. Brief-specific compositions (see Ingestion pipeline) all compose this wrapper — the wrapper is the atomic primitive; each MP4 is content placed inside it.

Variants

Single component, two surface variants (--dark / --light) that adjust border colour and fallback fill. Aspect ratio is locked at 16:9 to match the canonical 1920×1080 render canvas — the wrapper scales fluidly, the encoded MP4 is fixed.

on-dark

Canonical markup

<figure class="ds-motion-clip ds-motion-clip--dark" data-ds-motion-clip>
  <video class="ds-motion-clip__video"
         src="assets/motion/<slug>.mp4"
         poster="assets/motion/<slug>.poster.jpg"
         width="1920" height="1080"
         autoplay muted loop playsinline preload="metadata"
         aria-label="<one-sentence description of the composition>"></video>
  <figcaption class="ds-motion-clip__caption">
    Pre-rendered MP4 · 1920×1080 · 12s loop
  </figcaption>
</figure>

Usage rules

Reusable wrapper, brief-specific content. The wrapper itself is reusable across pages; the MP4 inside it is brief-specific. Each composition (Ingestion pipeline, Live stream → agent loop, etc.) ships as its own asset under assets/motion/ and is documented under Motion / Examples — not as a separate component.

16:9 aspect ratio is locked. The canonical render canvas is 1920×1080. Other aspect ratios require a separate component (deferred). The wrapper scales width fluidly via width: 100%; height: auto and preserves aspect via the video's intrinsic ratio.

All four autoplay attributes are required. autoplay muted loop playsinline — iOS Safari blocks autoplay without both muted and playsinline. loop assumes the composition is authored as a seamless loop (final frame returns to first frame's state).

aria-label required. One-sentence description of what the composition shows. Screen-reader users hear the label in place of the visual.

preload="metadata" by default. Fetches video headers (dimensions + duration) on page load; defers the body bytes until first visible-paint. Keeps page-load TTFB intact when motion clips sit below the fold.

Reduced-motion: pause at first frame. When prefers-reduced-motion: reduce matches, the wrapper removes the autoplay attribute, pauses the video, and resets currentTime to 0. The first frame stays visible (the composition's first frame is authored to be a coherent static state — Ingestion pipeline shows the system diagram at rest). Listener reacts to mid-session preference changes via matchMedia('change').

Pauses when offscreen. IntersectionObserver halts playback when the wrapper scrolls outside the viewport (rootMargin: 50px). Same pattern as .ds-ticker and .ds-particle-dome — saves GPU + bandwidth on long pages.

Fallback for failed load. If the MP4 fails to fetch, the wrapper falls back to the poster (if present) or a solid --neutral-dark / --surface-light fill. The [data-ds-motion-failed] attribute on the wrapper triggers fallback CSS — set programmatically on video element error event.

Decorative, never interactive. The video element carries pointer-events: none; clicks pass through. For a play-on-click variant — separate component, deferred.

Performance notes

Encoded MP4 size ≈ 2–5 MB per composition. H.264, target bitrate 2.5 Mbps, low-motion content. Cached aggressively via Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable (already covered by the existing /assets/(.*) rule in vercel.json).

0 KB JS on consuming page. Hyperframes is a build-time renderer — GSAP and any other animation library runs at render time, not at runtime. The host page just embeds a <video>.

Hardware-decoded H.264. Modern browsers decode H.264 on the GPU — negligible CPU cost vs. continuous JavaScript animation. Even mid-tier devices handle multiple concurrent motion clips without frame drops.

Motion / Examples / Ingestion pipeline

Ingestion pipeline

A 12-second pre-rendered MP4 motion organism. Brief: Upload from anywhere. Normalize formats with built-in transcoding. Stream globally in seconds, then index, search, and automate. Five multi-format video sources funnel into a single H.264 transcoder, then fan out to three downstream actions (index, search, automate). Orange packet dots traverse axis-aligned L-bend connector lines on continuous cycles. Authored in Hyperframes; rendered to MP4; embedded via Motion wrapper.

Preview

on-dark · 12s loop

Composition layout

Zonex rangeContent
Zone 1 — Upload sources96–5525 stacked source cards (Mobile / Desktop / Camera feed / API upload / Live stream). Each 92 px tall, 12 px gap.
Zone 2 — Transcoder620–1220Orange-bordered card with header (Adaptive H.264 transcoder), format-reduction band (MOV / MP4 / ProRes / HEVC / WebM → H.264), live stream status with rotating latency readout.
Zone 3 — Actions1288–18243 stacked action cards (Index frames / Search semantics / Automate workflows). Each 159 px tall, 16 px gap.
Connector trails552–620, 1220–1288SVG path underlays. 5 L-bend trails sources → transcoder; 3 straight trails transcoder → actions. White 18 % stroke, 1.5 px.
Footer caption96–1824, y=880Brief verbatim, body type 30 px, top-divider 1 px.

Motion grammar

ElementBehaviourCycleRepeats
Header status dotOpacity 0.65 ↔ 1, scale 0.85 ↔ 1.11.6 s7 yoyos (= 11.2 s)
Transcoder status pulseOpacity 0.6 ↔ 1, scale 0.9 ↔ 1.151.2 s9 yoyos (= 10.8 s)
Latency readoutCycles 212 → 198 → 224 → 207 ms3 s steps4 ticks across 12 s
Input packets (×5)L-bend traversal, axis-aligned1.45 s5 cycles, staggered 0–1.6 s
Output packets (×3)Straight horizontal traversal1.50 s5 cycles, staggered 0–1.4 s

Usage rules

Inline in narrative. Drop into product-page sections where the host narrative is "this is how ingestion works." Not a hero. Caption it. Width 720–960 px on desktop reads cleanly; wider reads as a hero (which it isn't); narrower loses source / action card readability.

One motion organism per fold. Two side-by-side reads as a video gallery; one per fold preserves the moment.

Don't trim or stop mid-cycle. The composition is paced for 12 s. Clipping the loop reads as broken.

Dark surface only at v0.1. The orange-on-charcoal vocabulary is built for --neutral-dark. A light variant requires a separate render with inverted contrast — deferred.

Source

Hyperframes composition. Source HTML + GSAP in the main project repo under hyperframes/v08-02-ingestion-pipeline/. See Hyperframes guide for the authoring workflow.

Render command. From the composition folder: npm run render. Wraps npx hyperframes render and copies the timestamped output to a stable filename. Sub-minute render on Apple Silicon.

Hosted asset. assets/motion/ingestion-pipeline.mp4 in this repo. Long-cached via the existing /assets/(.*) header rule.

Motion / Examples / Timeline scrubber

Timeline scrubber

Interactive + Animated. A live SVG/CSS illustration of natural-language search across a video timeline. Auto-cycles through 6 timestamped moments when idle; hover any thumbnail to override the cycle and scrub to that moment; mouse-out resumes the cycle. ≤6 KB inline JS, 0 build step. Brief: "Type a query, get timestamped moments." The first example of the system's Live illustrations authoring method, alongside Hyperframes for the heavier pre-rendered alternative.

Preview — hover a thumbnail

on-dark · interactive · hover overrides the autoplay cycle
Timeline 0 moments found

Behaviour breakdown

PhaseWhat happensDuration
Type"person wearing a safety vest" types character-by-character into the search bar2.2 s
ResolveMoment count animates 0 → 6, scrubber dots + thumbnails fade-in0.8 s
CycleActive state cycles through moments 1 → 6 with 0.85 s holds~5.5 s
Hover override (interactive)User hovers any thumbnail → active state snaps to that moment, autoplay pauses250 ms transition
ResumeMouse leaves the illustration → autoplay resumes from where it left off—
LoopAfter cycle completes, full reset + replay with 1.4 s pause1.4 s pause

Usage rules

Inline in narrative. Drop into product-page sections explaining natural-language search. Reads at 720–1080 px wide; below 480 px the thumbnail grid collapses to 2-col.

Hover responsiveness is the point. The reader's hand controls what they see — distinct from the Ingestion pipeline MP4 which plays the same 12 s loop regardless. Don't strip the hover interactivity to "simplify"; that defeats the purpose of choosing the live method over MP4.

Reduced-motion: snap to end state. When prefers-reduced-motion: reduce matches, the scrubber renders the final state immediately — query typed in full, 6 moments shown, first moment active, no animation. Hover override still works.

Pauses when offscreen. IntersectionObserver halts the cycle when the illustration scrolls outside the viewport (50 px rootMargin). Same primitive as .ds-motion-clip, .ds-particle-dome, .ds-ticker.

One per fold. Two interactive scrubbers on the same fold compete for the reader's hand.

Source method

Authored as inline SVG/HTML/CSS + ~80 lines of vanilla JS (no GSAP, no external animation library). Ships as part of index.html — no build step, no asset to copy. Total cost ~5 KB inline. For the authoring contract, see Live illustrations guide.

Motion / Authoring / Hyperframes guide

Hyperframes guide

How to author a new motion organism for VideoDB. Hyperframes is HeyGen's open-source build-time video framework — write HTML + CSS + GSAP, render to MP4 via headless Chrome + FFmpeg. Zero runtime cost on the consuming page; the rendered MP4 ships as a static asset. This guide covers the project structure, authoring contract, and design principles that keep new motion organisms consistent with the system.

When to reach for Hyperframes

Use Hyperframes when a brief calls for a complex, narratively-staged composition that would be heavy as live JS — multi-zone systems, packet flows across long paths, sustained ambient motion over 10+ seconds, anything where pixel-deterministic timing matters. Don't reach for it for simple hover states, single-element animations, or anything that fits inside the existing 200 ms decorative-motion cap — use CSS or the existing Motion atoms for those.

A Hyperframes organism is a brief-specific example, not a reusable component. The reusable primitive is Motion wrapper; the rendered MP4 is content.

Project structure

Each composition lives in its own folder outside this docs repo, in the main project under hyperframes/<slug>/:

hyperframes/
└── <slug>/                          # e.g. v08-02-ingestion-pipeline
    ├── index.html                   # HTML + CSS + GSAP composition
    ├── brand-tokens.css             # Shared design tokens (copied per folder)
    ├── meta.json                    # { id, name, description, spec }
    ├── package.json                 # npm run dev / lint / render
    ├── hyperframes.json             # Schema + paths config
    └── renders/                     # Output MP4s (gitignored or pinned)

Composition contract

PropertyValueWhy
Canvas1920 × 108016:9, matches Motion wrapper aspect ratio. Scales down fluidly on the consuming page.
Duration12.0 sLong enough to land a 3-act narrative; short enough to loop without fatigue. Authored as a seamless loop (final frame = first frame composition).
Frame rate30 fpsHigher rates inflate file size for marginal smoothness gain on motion-graphics content.
CodecH.264Hardware-decoded on all modern browsers. Target bitrate 2.5 Mbps for low-motion content.
Encoded size2–5 MB targetCacheable, fast over typical broadband. Keeps the consuming page's network budget honest.
Background--neutral-dark (#0A0A0A)Composition is authored against the system's dark canvas. Static first frame must read as a coherent system diagram even with motion paused.
Brand tokensCopy of brand-tokens.cssHyperframes serves the composition folder as the root — tokens must be self-contained.

Design principles

Axis-aligned packet motion. When packets traverse L-bend connector lines, GSAP keyframes must change left OR top between any two consecutive waypoints — never both. Diagonal interpolation cuts across the path geometry and breaks the "packet rides the wire" illusion. Three axis-aligned segments per L-bend: horizontal in → vertical bend → horizontal out.

Finite repeats. Hyperframes lints repeat: -1 as an error. Use finite counts that fill the 12 s duration — for a 1.45 s cycle: repeat: 4 (5 iterations × 1.45 = 7.25 s + staggered delays = ~9 s).

Centered packets via transform. transform: translate(-50%, -50%) on .packet so top/left set the centre of the dot. Without this, the dot's top-left corner sits on the connector line instead of the dot itself.

Paused timeline + global handle. Use gsap.timeline({ paused: true }) and store at window.__timelines["main"] = tl. Hyperframes drives the timeline; the composition shouldn't auto-play.

Clip metadata on every visible timed element. Every animated DOM node needs class="clip" + data-start + data-duration + data-track-index. Hyperframes uses these to plan the render.

Brand vocabulary. Compositions inherit the system's existing motion atoms — status pulse for live indicators, mono-uppercase eyebrows for chrome labels, hairline borders, orange accent reserved for the focal-flow element. New visual primitives invented inside a Hyperframes composition should later be promoted to system atoms if they're reused.

Render workflow

# Local preview (file:// in browser, no server)
cd hyperframes/<slug>
open index.html

# Or via Hyperframes studio (live editing UI)
npm run dev

# Lint composition before rendering
npx hyperframes@latest lint

# Render to MP4 (Apple Silicon: ~30–60 s)
npm run render
# Output: renders/<slug>_<timestamp>.mp4
#         renders/<slug>.mp4         (stable copy)

# Copy to design system repo
cp renders/<slug>.mp4 <design-system>/assets/motion/<slug>.mp4

# Commit MP4 alongside spec edits

Reduced-motion contract

Every Hyperframes-rendered motion organism inherits Motion wrapper's reduced-motion behaviour: when prefers-reduced-motion: reduce matches, the wrapper pauses the video at currentTime = 0 and removes autoplay. The first frame must therefore read as a coherent static composition — a system diagram, a layout snapshot, or a "settled state" of what the motion would show.

This is an authoring constraint: compose the first frame deliberately. Don't author a composition where the first frame is mid-animation (e.g. packets caught mid-flight). The reader who can't see motion still needs to understand what the composition shows.

Authoring checklist

  • 1920 × 1080 canvas, 30 fps, 12 s duration
  • Seamless loop (final frame = first frame composition)
  • First frame reads as a coherent static diagram
  • Brand tokens via brand-tokens.css import
  • No repeat: -1 — use finite counts
  • Packets centered via transform: translate(-50%, -50%)
  • Axis-aligned segment motion (no diagonals on L-bends)
  • Status pulses use the system's 1.2–1.6 s yoyo cadence
  • Every animated element has class="clip" + clip metadata
  • Lint passes (npx hyperframes lint) before render
  • Encoded MP4 ≤ 5 MB
  • Asset copied to assets/motion/<slug>.mp4
  • Spec entry added under Motion / Examples in design.md and index.html

Motion / Authoring / Live illustrations

Live illustrations guide

One of two motion-authoring methods in the system — the interactive counterpart to Hyperframes pre-rendered MP4s. Use this when the brief calls for interactivity — hover responses, scroll-driven state, anything the user's hand should drive. The composition ships as inline SVG / HTML / CSS + a small JS controller (≤ 5 KB), runs at runtime, and stays under the system's per-piece weight budget. The Timeline scrubber is the canonical example.

When to reach for Live illustrations

Brief signalMethod
User should control what they see (hover, click, scroll position)Live
≤ 5 KB inline, no asset to loadLive
Composition is a single dynamic surface (search field, scrubber, slider)Live
Auto-cycle when idle is acceptable as a fallback for non-interacting readersLive
Composition is a sustained 10+ s narrative with no user inputHyperframes
Multi-zone choreographed packet flows across long pathsHyperframes
0 KB JS at runtime on consuming page is a hard requirementHyperframes

When both could work, prefer Live — runtime-tweakable beats baked. Reach for Hyperframes when the composition would exceed the 5 KB inline budget or when you need pixel-deterministic timing that survives across browsers.

Project structure

Unlike Hyperframes, Live illustrations have no separate project folder. The composition lives inline in the consuming page (or in index.html of this design system). Three pieces in three places:

index.html (or consuming page)
├── <style> block       — CSS for the illustration's static + animated states
├── <section> markup    — HTML/SVG structure with data-attribute hooks
└── <script> block      — Vanilla JS controller (init function + IntersectionObserver)

Composition contract

PropertyValueWhy
Per-piece weight≤ 5 KB inline (CSS + HTML + JS combined)Lightweight is the point. If the composition needs more, the brief belongs in Hyperframes.
Library dependenciesNone at v0.1 — vanilla JS onlyThe system already loads Iconify for icons; no animation library beyond what the browser provides natively (CSS transitions, animateMotion, requestAnimationFrame).
InteractivityAt least one hover, click, or focus responseIf nothing is interactive, the brief belongs in Hyperframes or as a Motion atom.
Auto-cycle (idle behaviour)Optional but recommendedReaders who don't engage still see the composition demonstrate itself. The cycle pauses when the user starts driving.
Reduced-motionSnap to final / settled state, interactivity still worksThe composition stays legible without motion; user-driven state changes are not motion in the prefers-reduced-motion sense.
Offscreen pauseIntersectionObserver halts auto-cycle when scrolled outside viewportSaves CPU. Same primitive as .ds-ticker / .ds-particle-dome / .ds-motion-clip.
Class prefixds-<slug>__<part> + data-ds-<slug> hookMatches the rest of the system's naming. The init function targets the data-attribute, not the class.

Design principles

Compose from Motion atoms. Connector lines, arrows, packets, node containers, grid-frame texture — all live in Motion / Atoms. Reach for the atom before inventing a new primitive. The Timeline scrubber uses the grid-frame texture; Architecture flow uses nodes + connectors + arrows + packets. Family resemblance is the point.

Animated & Interactive together. An idle reader sees the autoplay (animated); an engaged reader takes over (interactive). The cycle should never block the user — hover always wins. See the animated vs interactive table for the canonical definitions.

Orange is the focal token. Same rule as Hyperframes — one orange element per composition (active dot, focal node, etc.). Other states use neutrals on the surface's contrast scale.

Transitions cap at 250 ms. Decorative state changes (hover focal, active dot scale, thumbnail border) stay under 250 ms — quick enough that the response feels immediate. Reach for slower curves (400 ms+) only for the auto-cycle's hold-and-release beats.

No external animation library at v0.1. If the brief needs GSAP-grade choreography, that's a Hyperframes signal — the live method stays small. Vanilla CSS transitions + small JS loops handle 95% of what a hover/click illustration needs.

Authoring workflow

  1. Sketch the static state first. What does the composition look like when nothing is moving? That's the reduced-motion fallback, the loading state, and the structure the JS will animate.
  2. Add the interactive state. Hover focal? Click toggles? Implement these with pure CSS transitions if possible (cheaper, no JS overhead).
  3. Wire the JS controller. Find the root via data-ds-<slug>; query children via data-i / data-state attributes (not class names — keeps CSS and JS targeting distinct).
  4. Add the auto-cycle. Pause it on user interaction (hover, focus, click); resume on mouse-leave / blur.
  5. Wrap in IntersectionObserver for offscreen pause. Reuse the existing system pattern.
  6. Implement prefers-reduced-motion branch: skip the cycle, render final state, keep interactivity active.
  7. Audit against the contract — weight under 5 KB, no external libs, atoms used where applicable, hover wins.

Authoring checklist

  • ≤ 5 KB inline (CSS + HTML + JS combined)
  • No external animation library
  • At least one hover / click / focus interaction
  • Auto-cycle (idle) + interactive override (engaged)
  • Pauses when offscreen (IntersectionObserver)
  • Reduced-motion: snap to final state, interactivity stays
  • Static first frame reads as coherent without motion
  • Composes Motion atoms (connectors, arrows, packets, nodes, grid frame) where applicable
  • One focal orange element only
  • Decorative transitions ≤ 250 ms
  • Class prefix ds-<slug>__; init hook data-ds-<slug>
  • Spec entry under Motion / Examples in this docs page

Organisms / Editorial primitives

Editorial primitives

Three inline patterns that show up inside long-form article body copy: Pull quote (orange-bar emphasis quote), Labeled callout (orange-labeled bulleted aside), and Decision list (numbered + kicker + body rows for documenting reasoning chains). Each is a discrete primitive — combined into one page since they're never used alone, only as members of the editorial toolkit.

Pull quote

3px orange left bar + italicized body. The inline-emphasis primitive for a single sentence that the reader should remember after they leave the article.

on-dark
Measure the bytes at the boundary that enforces the limit — not at the boundary you trust to be honest.
on-light
Measure the bytes at the boundary that enforces the limit — not at the boundary you trust to be honest.

Labeled callout

Soft-tint card with an orange mono label + dash-bulleted body list. Used for "Try this", "Debug these separately", or "Things to verify" asides that interrupt the main narrative.

on-dark
Debug these separately
  • Raw response bytes — what your handler returned before AWS touched it.
  • Transferred bytes — what AWS actually emitted on the wire (gzip applied).
  • Whether the request was sent with Accept-Encoding: gzip in the first place.
on-light
Debug these separately
  • Raw response bytes — what your handler returned before AWS touched it.
  • Transferred bytes — what AWS actually emitted on the wire (gzip applied).
  • Whether the request was sent with Accept-Encoding: gzip in the first place.

Decision list

Hairline-row table: numbered rank + uppercase kicker + body explanation. Documents a reasoning chain ("we chose X over Y because Z") with enough structure that the reader can scan, not just read.

on-dark
  1. 01 Structural layer Move heavy artifacts to S3 + return a presigned URL — keep the Lambda response under 1 MB by default.
  2. 02 Tactical layer Compress in the app when compressible JSON must be returned inline — don't trust API Gateway to negotiate gzip.
  3. 03 Observability Log both raw and transferred sizes on every response so the next 6 MB trap shows up in a chart, not in a customer ticket.
on-light
  1. 01 Structural layer Move heavy artifacts to S3 + return a presigned URL — keep the Lambda response under 1 MB by default.
  2. 02 Tactical layer Compress in the app when compressible JSON must be returned inline — don't trust API Gateway to negotiate gzip.
  3. 03 Observability Log both raw and transferred sizes on every response so the next 6 MB trap shows up in a chart, not in a customer ticket.

Usage rules

One primitive per editorial purpose. Pull quote = remember-this sentence. Callout = sidebar list. Decision list = ranked reasoning chain. Don't combine them or pick the wrong one — the visual differences carry semantic differences.

Sparingly. A long-form article uses 0–2 pull quotes, 1–3 callouts, 0–1 decision list. Beyond that the article reads as a doc, not as a narrative.

All three composed of atom-level patterns. Pull quote = blockquote + orange left border. Callout = small surface + Eyebrow-cadence label. Decision list = grid + Eyebrow-cadence kicker. No new primitives — they're recompositions.

Organisms / Tooltip

Tooltip

Hover / focus-within inline disclosure. The trigger word carries a dashed underline + cursor: help; hovering or keyboard-focusing it reveals a positioned tooltip 10px above. Pure CSS — no JS, no portal, no positioning library. Use for inline term definitions inside body copy, never for action affordances (use a button for those).

Variants

on-dark

Hover the dotted phrase to see Live agent-controlled playback over a video index. Sub-second latency. in action.

on-light

Hover the dotted phrase to see Live agent-controlled playback over a video index. Sub-second latency. in action.

Usage rules

For definition, not action. Tooltips explain unfamiliar terms. If the user has to do something, use a button or link — never hide an action behind a tooltip.

Trigger is a real <button>. Keyboard users tab to the button; :focus-within opens the tooltip the same way :hover does. A <span> trigger would skip keyboard support.

Short content only. Two lines max. If the explanation needs three lines, the term belongs in inline body copy, not a tooltip.

Positioned above, centered. 10px gap so the tooltip doesn't touch the trigger word. Centered horizontally so the eye returns to the same column. At narrow viewports the tooltip can overflow the parent — wrap it in overflow: visible ancestors.

Previous← Carousel NextNav dropdown →
Organisms / Nav dropdown

Nav dropdown

Hover-driven mega-menu. The menubar is a row of pill-on-hover triggers; each one with a submenu fades in a multi-column panel below it, with bordered icon tiles + label + description per row. Items without a submenu render as plain pill links. JS adds .is-open on mouseenter / focus and closes via a 120ms grace timer so the cursor can travel from trigger to panel without dropping.

Variants

on-dark

  • Build

    • Ingest Upload, capture, stream
    • Index Multimodal embeddings + scene-cut
    • Search Query by phrase, object, timecode

    Run

    • Stream RTMP, HLS, WebRTC
    • Edit Cut, splice, compose timelines
    • Playback Agent-controlled, sub-second

  • Resources

    • Docs SDK, REST, MCP server
    • Quickstart From key to first query in 5 min
    • Open source Director, CaptureSDK, examples

on-light

  • Build

    • Ingest Upload, capture, stream
    • Index Multimodal embeddings + scene-cut
    • Search Query by phrase, object, timecode

    Run

    • Stream RTMP, HLS, WebRTC
    • Edit Cut, splice, compose timelines
    • Playback Agent-controlled, sub-second

  • Resources

    • Docs SDK, REST, MCP server
    • Quickstart From key to first query in 5 min

Usage rules

Hover to open, 120ms grace to close. Cursor leaves the trigger → small timer fires before closing. This lets the user travel from trigger down to the panel diagonally without losing the menu mid-traverse. Touch users get tap-to-open (focus event triggers the same open path).

Pill bg is brand-orange at 10%, not a neutral scrim. The hover affordance ties the menubar to the brand instead of feeling like a generic chrome element. Same colour appears on both light and dark surfaces; the alpha carries the contrast.

Two to four columns per panel. One column reads like an oversized dropdown — fine for short menus (Developers above). Four+ columns push the panel past usable scan width — break into two menubar items instead.

Items without submenus render as plain pill links. Pricing / Customers above use the same trigger pill but no chevron, no panel. Keeps the menubar visually consistent — every item is a pill, half just happen to expand.

Icon tile is bordered, not orange-filled. 36×36 with a hairline border and currentColor icon. Hover lifts the border + adds a scrim wash, signalling "this row is hot" without re-using the action-orange that lives on CTAs.

Tabs

* What changed in v2.1 Two new modifiers: --scroll (horizontal scroll-snap on mobile when triggers ≥5) and .ds-tabgroup-shell (composition wrapper — outer grey shell + inner white pill). Mobile auto-promotion: when wrapped in a shell ≤820px, the outer shell drops its bg and pills switch to scroll-snap row with light-grey defaults + orange active.

Pill-shaped tab group with orange-on-active. The page-section switcher for "show me X / Y / Z" panels — the active tab carries the brand-orange fill because the choice is focal, not a quiet filter. Distinct from the Pill atom's Tablist composition, which uses white-on-charcoal for runtime / language switching where the tab is chrome, not the focal action.

Variants

on-dark
Six primitives compose into agent-shaped behaviours. One SDK, one mental model, one API surface — across ingest, index, search, stream, edit, and playback.
Usage-based pricing: pay only for hours indexed + bandwidth streamed. Free tier covers 10 hours / month; the Pro tier is metered linearly past that.

Usage rules

Orange-active = "this is the focal selection." Use Tabs when the user is being asked to make a meaningful choice between sections. Use the Pill atom's tablist when the tab is filter-like chrome (runtime switcher, framework picker).

Three to five tabs. Below three, use a Mode toggle. Above five, the tab row wraps and the orange-active state becomes hard to scan.

One panel visible at a time. The JS toggles hidden on each [data-ds-tabs-panel]; only one is unhidden. Don't show two panels concurrently — that's an accordion, not a tab group.

Arrow-key nav built in. Left / Right arrows move focus between triggers; Home / End jump to first / last. Standard tablist keyboard pattern.

Organisms / Announcement bar

Announcement bar

Top-of-page chrome strip. Eyebrow + body text + optional inline CTA link + close button. Production: sticky above the header at z-index: calc(var(--z-overlay) + 1). Three surface variants: Neutral (matches header tone — quiet, used for ongoing notes), Orange (loud, brand-orange surface — for product launches / beta access / event promos).

Variants

on-dark · neutral
V2.4 RTStream is now generally available. Read the announcement
on-light · neutral
V2.4 RTStream is now generally available. Read the announcement
orange · launch / event
Oct 15 · SF Join us at AI Engineer Summit — talks, demos, and free credits. Reserve a seat
on-dark · minimal (no CTA)
Scheduled maintenance Sunday 2am–4am PT. Some indexing may be delayed.

Usage rules

One announcement at a time. Stacking two bars cannibalises the attention of both — the user's eye does math instead of reading. If marketing and engineering both have something to say, the higher-stakes message wins this week.

Neutral for ongoing, Orange for launches. Use Neutral for things that live for weeks ("V2.4 GA", "New docs site"). Use Orange for time-bound events ("Join us at Summit Oct 15") and product moments that deserve a loud beat ("RTStream is live"). Orange should feel rare; if you reach for it weekly it stops landing.

Close button is always present. Dismissibility is non-negotiable — the user can't escape a sticky bar otherwise. Production: store the dismissed-bar ID in localStorage so it stays dismissed across page loads.

CTA link is inline, single arrow icon. The CTA is part of the sentence flow, not a button — "Read the announcement →". Buttons in an announcement bar feel heavy and start competing with the page-level primary action.

Eyebrow is the metadata, not the message. "V2.4" / "Oct 15 · SF" / "Beta" sit before the body text in orange mono-uppercase. They give the message a category at a glance.

Production: sticky above header. The bar lives at the very top of the viewport. Header sits below it. When the user dismisses the bar, the header slides up to fill the space — production should animate this transition rather than snap-jumping.

Usage rules

Fixed in production, static in the preview. The header is a top-of-page persistent element — production should add position: fixed; top: 0; left: 0; right: 0; z-index: var(--z-overlay); and pad the content area by a measured --ds-header-h custom prop. The preview keeps it inline so it doesn't float above the docs chrome.

Backdrop blur reads through content on scroll. 12px blur + 80% opacity surface gives the content underneath a soft scrim without going opaque — the page reads as one continuous surface with a chrome plate over it.

One primary CTA, one ghost. "Get API key" is the orange primary; "Sign in" is the ghost utility. Adding a second primary CTA dilutes the conversion path. If marketing wants a second emphasis (e.g. "Book a demo"), promote it inside the Platform dropdown, not on the bar.

Brand mark is 26px square with the brand-orange fill. Mirrors the favicon. Don't drop in the wordmark-only logo here — at 22px height the wordmark reads as a thin slate; the mark + wordmark composition holds presence at chrome scale.

Mobile collapses centre + sign-in into a hamburger. Below 1024px the centre nav and sign-in link hide; the hamburger button appears next to "Get API key" and opens a full-height drawer (a Drawer organism / modal-nav primitive — not implemented yet; the trigger is the visible state).

Announcement bar sits above the header. When both are stacked, the announcement bar at z-index: calc(var(--z-overlay) + 1); header sits below at --z-overlay. Dismissing the bar slides the header up to fill the space.

Usage rules

Row variant: 3 or 4 cells. Two cells reads as a side-by-side, not a row. Five or more compresses the values past readability — use a table instead.

Column variant: 3 cells. Sits as a side panel beside body copy or in narrow content folds. More than 3 in a column gets too tall.

Callout metric

A single quantitative claim, sized to land as a section-level moment. Display-scale number + supporting clause + small mono provenance note. Used between paragraphs in long-form narrative to interrupt the prose with a measured fact — softer than a hero stat row, louder than inline text.

Variants

on-dark · staged reveal
240ms

SOURCE · /benchmarks/p95-latency

Reveal sequence

BeatElementTiming
0 msOrange left bar draws top → bottom350 ms ease-out
350 msContainer background tints in400 ms ease-out

Usage rules

One per fold. Two callouts in the same section compete; one lands.

Provenance is required. The mono note at the bottom names the source — a benchmark, a study, a dataset, an internal cost model. Without it, the number reads as marketing.

Body clause supports the number. What's being measured, against what, when. Keep it under two lines.

Data Viz / Stats & metrics / Before / after

Before / after comparison

Two-cell layout showing a measured delta — old metric on the left in muted type, new metric on the right at full scale, with an arrow + change indicator between them. The system's canonical "we improved X by Y" composition.

Variants

on-dark · with jackpot animation on viewport reveal
BEFORE · v1 retrieval
1,840ms
−87%
AFTER · v2 multimodal
1,840ms

Jackpot animation

On viewport reveal, the after value starts at the before number and animates down (or up, depending on direction) to its target — like a slot-machine readout settling into place. Duration 1.4 s, ease-out, with the digits rolling at decreasing speed. The delta arrow + percent fade in slightly ahead so the reader sees "−87%" before the number lands. One-shot. prefers-reduced-motion: reduce renders the final number with no roll.

Usage rules

Direction of improvement matters. Lower-is-better metrics show a negative percent change (latency, cost, error rate). Higher-is-better shows positive (recall, throughput). The arrow direction stays right-pointing; the percent sign carries the polarity.

Same unit on both sides. Comparing ms-to-ms, %-to-%, count-to-count. Don't mix units.

Usage rules

Bars use orange only for the focal row. One bar highlighted per chart. Highlighting two or more breaks the focal hierarchy. Use --bar--focal modifier.

Scroll-reveal bar growth is sanctioned. Bars grow from 0 → target width on viewport entry (700 ms ease-out, 80 ms stagger per row). One-shot — no re-trigger on scroll-back. Honours prefers-reduced-motion: reduce (renders the final state immediately). Count-up animations on numeric values stay forbidden — labels and values land static; only the bar fills animate.

Label widths cap at 25%. Long labels truncate with ellipsis at this width to preserve track width. If labels need more space, switch to a column chart with rotated labels.

Data Viz / Diagrams / Architecture flow

Architecture flow

Declarative system architecture diagram — boxes (nodes) connected by labelled edges, with continuous packet flow tokens traversing each connection. Reads as a system schematic: which components talk to which, in what direction, carrying what data. Rendered live via SVG (no MP4 baseline — this is interactive at runtime, unlike Ingestion pipeline which ships as a pre-rendered organism).

Variants

on-dark · 4 nodes · 4 edges · continuous packet flow
on-light · same diagram · continuous packet flow

Usage rules

Live SVG, not Hyperframes MP4. This is an interactive component — packet flow is driven by <animateMotion> in the browser. For a pre-rendered narrative version with brief-specific zones and a fixed 12 s composition, use Ingestion pipeline (Motion organism) instead.

Continuous packet flow, not staged. Tokens travel each edge on independent loops with staggered delays — the system reads as "always running", not "playing an animation." Per the system's functional motion exemption: the loop IS the component.

Orange reserved for the focal node. Typically VideoDB itself (the centre of the diagram). Other nodes use hairline neutral borders. No second-tier colour coding.

Cap at 6 nodes / 8 edges. Above this density, edge crossings become hard to read at typical column widths. Split into two diagrams or use a layered Stack diagram instead (deferred component).

Pauses when offscreen. SVG <animateMotion> wrapped in IntersectionObserver — same pattern as .ds-ticker, .ds-particle-dome, .ds-motion-clip.

Templates / Section structure

Section structure

The page-section primitive. Every other template sits on this. Three layers: .ds-section (surface + vertical rhythm), .ds-frame (max-width container with railed gutter borders), .ds-col-offset (12-col grid that reserves a left rail for the section-code label + a right column for body content). Section background switches by surface modifier (--dark / --light). Ported from cleanup .bk-section / .bk-frame / .bk-col-offset.

Anatomy

Section wraps Frame wraps Col-offset wraps the two columns. The left column carries the mono-uppercase section code label ("01 / Hero"); the right column holds the content — heading + lead + body composition. The Frame's left/right hairline borders give the page its railed edge.

Section

Section structure example.

Left column is the mono-uppercase code label. Right column carries the section heading + lead + whatever organisms the section composes. The Frame's vertical hairlines give the page its railed edge.

Body content goes here. This is where you compose Cards, Tickers, Editorial primitives, etc. — any organism that fits the section's intent.

on-light

Section

Same shell, light surface.

All inner colours derive from the surface modifier — text, borders, code label all flip together. No per-element overrides needed.

Body content. Light-surface sections work the same way — drop your organisms inside the right column.

Usage rules

Every marketing page section uses this shell. Hero, Problem/Solution, Lifecycle, Closing CTA — all wrap their content in .ds-section > .ds-frame > .ds-col-offset. The shell carries the vertical rhythm + railed edges; the inner column carries the content. Consistency across sections comes for free.

Section code label is the navigation kicker. Two lines: number / word ("03 / Lifecycle"). Sits in the left column at the top of the section. Acts as a poor-man's IA breadcrumb when the user is scanning.

Frame max-width is 1200px. Above 1200px the section pads outward with the body bg — the railed hairlines define the content edge, not the viewport edge. This is what gives the kit its desktop "framed page" feel.

Col-offset is responsive. Single column below 768px (code label stacks above content); 3fr/9fr at tablet; 2fr/10fr at desktop. The left rail is narrower at larger sizes because the body needs the space.

Section padding is 96px top/bottom. All sections breathe the same. Don't override per-section unless the design intent specifically requires a tighter or looser cadence (e.g. a single-line closing band might warrant 64px).

Usage rules

Pick by what you want the user to absorb first. Default (A) for performance / scale with small numeric stats. Centered-with-code (B) for "try it now" moments. Big-stats (C) for homepage scale-pitch where the numbers ARE the headline. With-image-ticker (D) when the value-prop is visual — "look what teams have built with us." Animated (E) when brand presence matters more than scan speed — reach for the particle dome only on the focal marketing hero, not on inner pages.

One hero per page, always at the top. The hero owns the page-opener moment. A second hero further down is a section heading + visual, not a hero.

Two-tone display heading is the default brand voice. First line is the assertion, second line (wrapped in __display-second) is the qualifier in a muted tone.

Live pill on A + C, eyebrow on B + D + E. The pill carries a real-time signal (current release, GA, beta). The eyebrow is editorial context — release dot + version + short note for Variants D and E.

Stats strip vs big stats. Small mono stats (Variant A): 4 short numbers in a horizontal strip. Big stats (C): 4 display-scale numbers as the visual anchor. Pick by how loud the numbers should be.

CTA pair on A + C + D + E, single CTA on Centered-with-code (B). The centered B variant has the code block as the secondary affordance — a ghost button next to the primary would compete with the code reveal.

Animated variant performance budget. Variant E loads Three.js (~150 KB gzipped) on first paint. Use it only on pages where the brand moment is worth that weight — the home page, the product hero, key marketing surfaces. Inner pages (docs, pricing, content) should use the static variants. See Particle dome for the GPU + reduced-motion notes.

← Field Notes / Media Infra

The hidden 6 MB Lambda trap: compression and payload limits

When Postman lies and AWS rejects: a story about boundary measurement and the negotiation that happens too late.

Rohit Garg · Field note · 5 min

In this note

  • Problem
  • The Lambda boundary
  • Compression negotiation
  • The gotcha in testing
  • Fix
  • What changed
  • Production lesson

The problem. We were returning a 6.4 MB JSON blob from a Lambda function via API Gateway. The function ran clean, the response built clean, then API Gateway rejected the payload with a generic 500. Postman, locally proxying around API Gateway, returned the response just fine — so we shipped it. It only broke in production, and only intermittently.

The root cause turned out to be a boundary mismatch: Lambda's response limit is 6 MB raw, but API Gateway only negotiates compression after Lambda has already returned the payload. So the raw size check runs first, fails, and the gzip step that would have brought the blob to 1.8 MB never runs.

The fix was two-fold: gzip in the Lambda function itself before returning (using the runtime's compression library), and add a sanity check that returns a 413 with retry guidance when the raw payload exceeds 5.5 MB. The retry guidance points to a streaming endpoint we built for exactly this case.

…the rest of the article body would continue here. This is the structural pattern: leading paragraph + body paragraphs + ending nav below.

← Engineering / Indexing internals

How we cut multimodal index build time by 6×

Re-architecting the indexer to pipeline embedding generation, scene-cut, and transcript alignment into one pass.

Ashutosh Trivedi · Engineering · 8 min

In this note

  • The constraint
  • No real data dependency
  • Pipelining the three stages
  • Memory ceiling vs throughput
  • Results

The constraint. Before the rewrite, indexing a one-hour video took ~14 minutes wall-clock. Embeddings ran serial after scene-cut, scene-cut ran serial after transcript. Each stage waited for the previous one's full output before kicking off.

We knew the three workloads had no actual data dependency between them — embeddings need raw frames, scene-cut needs raw frames, transcripts need audio. None of them needs another's output. The serial pipeline was an artifact of the original v1 codepath, not a constraint.

…the rest of the article body would continue here. Same shell, dark surface.

← Back to Engineering

Usage rules

Article hero sits above the body, not inside it. The hero is a discrete top-of-article block (kicker / title / lead / byline). The two-column body grid starts below it. Don't nest the hero inside the prose column — the TOC needs to span the full body height.

TOC is sticky at desktop, stacks above at mobile. Below 1024px the grid collapses to a single column and the TOC moves above the body (so the user sees the contents before diving in). Sticky positioning only kicks in at desktop where there's vertical real estate for it.

Body type is 17px / 1.7. Comfortable for long-form reading — bigger than 14px UI text but not so big that lines run too wide at the constrained column width. Paragraph spacing is 18px (slightly more than the line height for visual rhythm).

Ending nav is mono-uppercase + back-arrow. Single sticky pattern across the editorial section. Hover lifts to orange + bumps the gap. Sits inside the article body, not below the grid — it's part of the reading experience, not chrome around it.

Compose Editorial primitives inside the body. Pull quote / Labeled callout / Decision list / Highlight all live in the prose column. Don't reach for one-off blockquote / aside / pre styling — the Editorial primitives carry the brand's voice.

Feature and benefit grid UPDATED v2.2.1

A 3-up × 2-row grid of icon + title + body cards. The canonical layout for "here's what the platform does" or "here's what each capability gives you" sections. Replaces v2.0's Feature grid pattern; the new canonical variant ports the homepage Platform-section design.

Live preview · dark surface (homepage variant)

The platform

A single backend for the
entire video lifecycle.

Six primitives that compose. Use one, use all of them. The same SDK across files, live streams, cameras, screen capture, and datasets.

Ingest

URL, upload, RTSP, ONVIF, RTMP, screen and audio capture, webhook, dataset. One ingestion path, normalized for everything that comes after.

Index

Reusable, additive structures over media: scenes, speech, objects, embeddings, brands, talent, custom domain events. Composable at query time.

Memory

Scene-level memory across sessions, archives, and live workloads. Re-indexable forever. Scoped per user, agent, workspace, or fleet.

Search

Sub-second, semantic + structured search across petabyte archives. Every hit is a playable clip, materialized in milliseconds.

Director

Cut, compose, dub, subtitle, reframe, brand — by code, not by drag-and-drop. The agentic skill SDK for media editing.

RTStream

HLS, WebSocket, agent-callable URLs. Output fits the consuming system — live cameras, calls, and screens at 1,000+ feed scale.

Usage rules

Intro left, grid right. Eye scans the framing first (left column), then dives into the verticals (right column). Don't flip the order — "here are the industries / here's why we built for them" reads backwards if cards come first.

5fr / 7fr split at desktop. Intro gets just under half the column, cards get the larger share so the 2×3 grid breathes. Below 1024px the grid collapses to single column (intro stacks above cards).

6 tiles in a 2×3 grid is the sweet spot. Industries / verticals lists usually land at 5–7 items; 6 fits cleanly. Below 4, the grid feels lonely — use a CTA pair instead. Above 8, split into categories.

Bare icon, not bg-tile. The --icon-bare modifier on Feature tile drops the icon's 40×40 bg square and leaves the icon standing alone. Reads as a content marker rather than chrome. Distinct from Feature and benefit grid UPDATED template which uses the bg-tile look for compact value-prop lists.

Eyebrow carries the section identity. Small orange dot + mono-uppercase label (e.g. "Industries", "Use cases", "Customers"). The dot is brand colour without overpowering — signals "this is a category section".

One Arrow CTA only. Single link out of the section ("Enterprise", "See all", "Talk to sales"). The tiles themselves can be linked too, but the intro CTA is the canonical out-link.

Templates / Sync compare

Sync compare

Two-column paired-row compare with synchronised hover. Hovering or focusing any row on one side highlights its paired row on the other (matched by data-row attribute). Used when you want users to compare across columns at the row level, not the column level — the comparison is the pair, not the cell. Right column uses a soft warm-orange tint for the "good" side. Ported from cleanup .bk-sync-compare with a new initSyncCompare() JS controller.

Usage rules

Pair rows by data-row attribute. Each row carries data-row="key"; rows sharing a key get highlighted together on hover or focus. Keys are arbitrary — pick whatever maps the rows semantically (storage / transcode / speech / etc.).

Use when the comparison is row-level, not column-level. If the user should walk down both columns in parallel ("for storage, today uses X, VideoDB uses Y"), Sync compare is the pattern. If the comparison is two distinct value-stacks viewed side-by-side, use Problem / Solution instead.

Keyboard parity built in. Each row gets tabindex="0" automatically — tab through to highlight pairs without needing a mouse. Focus highlights the pair the same way hover does.

Right column uses warm-orange tint, not full orange. The brand-orange treatment on the right card in Problem / Solution would compete with the orange highlight on hovered pairs. Soft tint keeps the highlight as the focal interaction.

5–7 rows per column. Below 5, the pairs read trivially. Above 7, the user loses track of which key maps where. Keep it scannable.

Animated flow

One flowing connector per section. Animate the single focal data path; leave structural connectors static so the diagram reads as signal, not ornament.

Implementation. Apply ds-diagram__connector to one SVG <path>. It uses stroke-dasharray plus the stream-flow keyframe to animate stroke-dashoffset. Add ds-diagram__connector--reverse to use stream-flow-rev for response paths.

Usage rules

Two cards is the sweet spot. Side-by-side compare reads cleanly. One card alone feels lonely; three+ cards on a row compress the rows too tight to scan.

Three row states. Default (neutral) for normal data. is-fail (orange tint + orange dot + orange text) for the row that broke. is-success (lifted neutral) for rows that completed under budget. Don't mix more than two states per card — the eye can only track so much state.

Progress bar can exceed 100%. Setting width: 106% on the fill bar signals overflow visually — the bar runs past its own track edge. Pair with is-fail rows to make the overflow narrative consistent.

Tick labels in the head row are mono-uppercase, max 3 words each. Pattern: <active label> on the left, <muted descriptor> on the right. Two ticks total — more and the head becomes a paragraph.

Use for technical / data-narrative content. Postmortem write-ups, performance comparisons, capacity diagrams. Not for marketing pages — the dot-grid + mono labels read as engineering, not pitch.

Templates / Roadmap timeline

Roadmap timeline

Horizontal milestone-bar infographic. Two-tone mission heading at the top + segmented timeline bar below with milestone labels alternating above and below the bar. Segments tint progressively lighter from left (oldest) to right (newest); the segment carrying .is-active paints brand orange to anchor "you are here now". Used for company roadmap, product history, fundraise journey, release-by-release infographics — anywhere a sequence of dated milestones reads better as a horizontal bar than a vertical changelog. Composes Section heading typography + new .ds-timeline-roadmap template-internal classes.

Usage rules

Alternate labels above / below the bar. Reading order goes left-to-right along the bar; above/below alternation keeps adjacent labels from crowding each other. Even-indexed milestones (1st / 3rd / 5th) go below; odd-indexed (2nd / 4th / 6th) go above. Or invert it — the pattern works either way as long as it alternates.

One segment per milestone. Segments are the visual rhythm; each one represents a chapter between two dates. 5–8 segments is the sweet spot. Below 5 the bar reads as too short for a roadmap; above 8 the labels start running into each other on tablet.

Default is 6 columns. Override via inline style="--cols: 5" on .ds-timeline-roadmap to change segment count. The grid keeps labels + segments aligned regardless.

One .is-active segment, always. Typically the rightmost ("we are here now"). The brand-orange anchor tells the user where the story currently sits. Multiple active segments dilute the signal.

Segments tint progressively brighter / darker. Left = oldest, dimmest. Right = newest, brightest. Reads as "history warming up to the present." The active segment overrides the tint with brand orange.

Mission heading is two-tone, not centered. Left-aligned heading with the opening assertion in default text colour and the qualifier in the muted second tone (--text-on-*-second). Centered headings work too but read more "section-opener" than "mission statement."

Milestone label = date + title, dashed underline. Date is mono-uppercase (subtle), title is Geist 14px with a dashed underline that mirrors a link affordance. In production, each title should link to a deeper page (blog post about the milestone, release notes, etc.).

Use for roadmap / company history / release-by-release. Not for changelog (use Carousel organism for inline release-notes), not for steps / workflow (use Lifecycle grid). The horizontal-bar metaphor reads as "journey through time" specifically.

Usage rules

Sits directly above the Footer. The Footer is brand + compliance chrome (formal). Pre-footer socials is the human invitation right before that ("come find us") — tone shift between the two surfaces is intentional.

4–6 tiles in the grid. 6 is the screenshot pattern (GitHub / Discord / X / YouTube / Docs / Blog). Fewer than 4 reads as a weak CTA strip — reach for the Footer's social icon row instead.

Centered heading, no eyebrow. Pattern consistent with the centered template variants: heading + short subtitle, nothing else above. The grid IS the chrome.

Each tile = one surface. Don't mix surface-types with categories (e.g. "Tutorials" alongside "GitHub"). The pattern is "where we live online" — one tile per platform / surface.

Meta is one line, <6 words. "3100+ Stars", "@videodb", "Workshops & demos" — numeric proof or short descriptor only.

v2.1.1 patch · Changelog

v2.1.1 — footer chevron desktop-leak fix

Minor patch. Single-rule fix to the ds-footer organism (Editorial variant, vh-footer accordion wrapper). Released 2026-05-22.

Scope — one CSS-only change. No new components, no new modifiers, no markup changes. Backwards-compatible with v2.1 consumers.

The bug

The .vh-footer__nav-chevron span — the accordion-trigger affordance attached to each .vh-footer__nav-title — was rendering on desktop. Its only styling lived inside @media (max-width: 768px), but the span itself was in the markup unconditionally. So above 768px the chevron icon leaked next to each section label:

PLATFORM ⌄
SOLUTIONS ⌄
DEVELOPERS ⌄
COMPANY  ⌄

Worth noting alongside this bug: a separate desktop overlap issue between the floating .vh-view-toggle (HUMAN / MACHINE pill) and the footer's .ds-footer__status pulse ("ALL SYSTEMS OPERATIONAL") clipping. Tracked separately — the pinning logic that lifts the toggle above the footer prelude is currently gated to (max-width: 768px).

The fix

Default the chevron to display: none on desktop and reset the title's cursor outside the mobile media query. The existing mobile rule (display: inline-flex inside @media (max-width: 768px)) overrides as before — mobile accordion behavior unchanged.

/* Desktop default — hide the accordion chevron + trigger affordance.
   Mobile media query re-enables both as an accordion. */
.vh-footer .vh-footer__nav-chevron { display: none; }
.vh-footer .vh-footer__nav-title { cursor: default; }

Rollout

Applied to all 8 pages on the page/Platform branch of videodb-website:

  • index.html
  • platform.html
  • developers.html
  • company.html
  • agentic-perception.html
  • real-time-monitoring.html
  • programmable-media.html
  • world-model-data.html

Affected component

  • ds-footer — Editorial variant only. Directory variant doesn't use the vh-footer accordion wrapper and is unaffected.

Migration

None required. Drop the two-rule CSS block into any page that still ships the leaky chevron — same pattern across every consumer.

v2.1 patch · Changelog

v2.1 — mobile-responsive patch round

Promoted from page-scoped overrides on videodb-website/platform.html (branch page/Platform). 12 base-rule updates, 9 new modifiers, 3 net-new components, 8 new conventions.

Legend — sidebar markers: NEW = brand-new component, modifier, or template added in v2.1. * = existing component received base-rule updates, new modifiers, or stale-component removal in v2.1 (see each page for details).

v2.1 patch round — what's verified working in the showcase

  • Live interactions wired on every NEW preview that has a state mechanic: menu-toggle (click), tabs nested-pill (click pill OR hover card → focus + ARIA-selected sync across 6 primitives), mobile-drawer-top-down (open-state mockup w/ Solutions expanded), section-heading-split (static markup, no JS needed).
  • Responsive preview containers on every component that has a mobile variant: hero-split (≥768 / <768 watermark), trust-band (auto-chip ≤640), mode-grid (1-col ≤768), mobile-drawer-top-down (phone-frame at 280–380px). Each uses CSS resize: horizontal — drag the bottom-right handle on the preview container to test responsive behavior in-place.
  • Per-page change notes below each *-marked component's H1 — orange-bordered callout listing the specific selectors / values / new modifiers added in v2.1.
  • Old #organisms/mobile-drawer route consolidated — content replaced with a redirect stub pointing to mobile-drawer-top-down. Removed from sidebar; route preserved for legacy bookmarks.

Stale components removed / superseded

  • Mobile drawer side-slide pattern — preserved on organisms/mobile-drawer for legacy reference; the canonical pattern for new pages is now --top-down. The default solar:close-circle-linear in-panel close icon is superseded by the new .ds-menu-toggle atom (CSS-only hamburger ↔ X morph).
  • In-panel drawer header (logo + close button) — hidden on --top-down. The site header stays visible and handles both roles.
  • [hidden] display:none snap on .ds-mobile-drawer__sub-list — replaced with a max-height transition (0 ↔ 520px, 280–320ms cubic) for accordion behavior.
  • Inline-style "trust band" pattern — promoted to a proper .ds-trust-band molecule. Page-scoped inline-style soup should be removed from consumers.
  • Iconify solar:hamburger-menu-linear in header — superseded by .ds-menu-toggle. Removes the library-mix (Solar hamburger + Solar close-circle were different glyph families).
  • overflow-x: hidden on html/body — replaced with overflow-x: clip. hidden creates a scrollport that breaks position: sticky on the header.
  • Consumer-side canvas-clamp boilerplate — every page that used .ascii-illustration or .ds-motion-clip had to re-implement the canvas scale-down. Now baked into the base rule.
  • Fixed-padding sections + frames on mobile — .ds-section { padding: 96px 0 } and .ds-frame { padding: 0 32px } previously had no mobile ladder. Page-scoped overrides accumulated everywhere. Now standardized via the v2.1 mobile padding ladders.

New atoms

  • .ds-menu-toggle — CSS-only hamburger ↔ X icon (atom #18).

New molecules

  • .ds-trust-band — compliance / trust pill row (molecule #13).
  • .ds-mode-grid — 2-up mixed light/dark card grid with code-line strip (molecule #14).
  • .ds-section-heading--split — asymmetric heading-left + lead-right modifier.

New organism modifiers

  • .ds-tabgroup--scroll — horizontal scroll-snap on mobile.
  • .ds-tabgroup-shell — nested-pill (outer grey shell + inner white pill).
  • .ds-mobile-drawer--top-down — top-to-bottom slide, behind navbar, stagger items.
  • .ds-hero--split — copy-left / illustration-right hero (6th variant).

Critical fixes

  • .ds-btn + .ds-header-nav__menu-trigger now enforce 44×44 touch-target minimum (Apple HIG / WCAG).
  • html, body { overflow-x: clip } ≤640 — replaces hidden which breaks position: sticky.
  • Canvas-clamp baked into .ascii-illustration and .ds-motion-clip — no more 1440px renderer overflows.
  • .ds-mobile-drawer__sub-list accordion now uses max-height transition instead of [hidden] display:none snap.

v2.2.1 — cleanup + tweaks batch NEW

Structural cleanup of the templates and organisms inventory + follow-up polish on v2.2.0 additions. No net-new components — this round removes deprecated entries, refreshes 3 existing components to match the live videodb-website implementation, and applies a series of design-debt fixes (adaptive testimonial card, side rails removed globally, sync compare restored, sidebar restructured).

Deleted

  • Lifecycle grid (template) — redundant with Feature and benefit grid + Industries grid.
  • Platform overview (template) — redundant with the new Feature and benefit grid.
  • Use case row (template) — low-utility pattern, no live consumers.
  • ds-cta-band (organism) — superseded by the new Closing CTA — particle field template (v2.2.0). Existing pages should migrate.

Renamed / reworked

  • Feature grid → Feature and benefit grid. Existing variants dropped; new canonical variant uses the homepage Platform section (6-card icon + title + body grid). Both light + dark surfaces.
  • Problem / Solution — variant replaced with the homepage Problem section pair (2× ds-compare-card with circular bullets, hairline row separators, no gradients, status pill at the bottom). Both light + dark.
  • ds-pricing-card Variant B — replaced with the homepage Deployment cards (3-card bracket-headed pattern with circular bullets, row hairlines between features, prominent CTA at the bottom). Both light + dark.
  • ds-logo-card — the --grid variant added in v2.2.0 is now documented inside the main Logo card preview (no standalone sidebar entry). Both Variant A (List) and Variant B (Grid) ship with light + dark previews.

Tweaks applied (post-initial cut)

  • .ds-frame side rails removed globally. Matches the homepage's Phase 1 rail-removal decision. The design system docs no longer render hairlines on the left + right edges of .ds-frame.
  • .ds-compare-card--good gradient dropped. Previously had a faint orange linear-gradient background. New canonical: white (or charcoal on dark) background + orange border. Only the border carries the "this is the solution" semantic.
  • .ds-compare-card__rows flex: 1. Combined with margin-top: auto on the bottom .ds-pill-status, the pill anchors to the bottom of the card regardless of how few rows are present. Cards in a pair stay vertically aligned.
  • .ds-testimonial-card adaptive height. Switched from fixed-height + absolute-positioned slide-up to grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr. No clipping at any description length; card grows naturally on hover.
  • Logo card Variant A — light surface preview added. Now shows dark + light, matching Variant B.
  • Sync compare preview restored. Was accidentally removed during the bulk-delete pass. Rebuilt with the canonical 2-column synchronised-hover compare layout + working initSyncCompare() JS controller + 5-rule Usage rules section.
  • Customer wall preview restored. Reverted to the full Variant A (Static grid) + Variant B (Ticker) + Usage rules layout. The intermediate --clean variant was an over-simplification.
  • Sidebar restructured. Three separate version groups (v2.2.0 / v2.1.1 / v2.1) consolidated into a single collapsible Changelog section at the top. v2.1 component links (Menu toggle, Trust band, Mode grid, etc.) redistributed to their proper module sidebar groups with NEW badges.
  • Anatomy code blocks removed from v2.2.x preview pages. design.md remains the canonical HTML source; preview pages now focus on rendered components + behavior notes + use-when guidance.

Counts after v2.2.1

  • Atoms: 19 (no change)
  • Molecules: 15 (no change)
  • Organisms: 39 → 38 (ds-cta-band removed)
  • Templates: 16 → 13 (Lifecycle grid, Platform overview, Use case row removed; Feature grid renamed in place to Feature and benefit grid)
  • Conventions: 10 (no change)

Migration

  • Lifecycle grid / Platform overview / Use case row — adopt Feature and benefit grid as the closest equivalent.
  • Feature grid → Feature and benefit grid — rename the template reference. Existing markup may need an update to the new canonical variant if the page wants the homepage Platform-section look.
  • ds-cta-band — adopt the new Closing CTA — particle field template (§3.7) for closing CTAs. The old markup is preserved on legacy pages but should not be used for new builds.

Full canonical spec for every change lives in docs/atomic-design-system/design.md under the v2.2.1 changelog section.

Changelog · v2.2.0

v2.2.0 — homepage promotion batch NEW

Feature round driven by the videodb-website homepage refinement cycle (Phase 2). Promoted page-scoped overrides to canonical DS components: 2 new atoms, 1 new molecule, 1 new variant on ds-logo-card, 1 new organism in the Cards subgroup, 2 new templates, and 2 new system-wide conventions.

What's new — components

  • .ds-skip-link — keyboard skip-to-main-content link (atom #19)
  • .ds-feature-list — stacked feature list with hairline-separated rows (molecule #15)
  • .ds-testimonial-card — single-layer case-study card with slide-up description (organism, Cards subgroup #9)
  • Sticky scroll — scroll-pinned narrative section with progress dots (template #14)
  • Closing CTA — particle field — full-bleed closer with 2D canvas particle background (template #15)
  • Onboarding — "install + show me code" fold with bordered frame around feature list + animated code block (template #16)

What's new — conventions

  • C9 — inert for non-active panels. Visual visibility and tab order must match. Apply inert to hidden-via-CSS panels in scroll-coupled, tabbed, or modal-trapped UIs.
  • C10 — Pointer-coarse fallback for hover-revealed content. Anything that reveals on hover must have a @media (pointer: coarse) rule keeping it visible at rest on touch devices.

Why these, why now

Each candidate was hand-picked from the homepage vh-* overrides pool — the prefix originally meant "VideoDB homepage" and was deliberately separate from ds-*. After shipping the homepage, the patterns below proved generally reusable (any future page would benefit from them) and were promoted into the design system. Site-only patterns (hero pill weakening, eyebrow tweaks, mobile-only specifics) remain site-scoped in videodb-website/src/partials/css_site_overrides.html.

Migration notes

None required. All v2.2.0 additions are net-new components or net-new variants — no breaking changes, no deprecations. The videodb-website homepage continues to use its vh-* override classes as before (per the v2.2.0 charter: documentation only, website unchanged).

3.1 Atoms · 19 of 20

Skip link NEW v2.2

Standard a11y skip-to-main-content link. Rests at the top-left, hidden (faded out and nudged down) until keyboard-focused — then it fades in and slides up from below into place. Brand-orange treatment so it reads as a system signal, not a stray browser default.

Preview · interactive — hover the box, or Tab to focus the link

on-dark · hover the box (or Tab) — the orange link slides up from below. Skip to main content

Preview · light variant — dark-grey button on a light surface

on-light · .ds-skip-link--on-light · hover (or Tab) — the dark-grey link slides up from below. Skip to main content

Behavior

Default state: positioned absolute at top: 16px (top-left) but hidden — opacity: 0, nudged down translateY(10px), and pointer-events: none so the invisible link can't intercept clicks. Focus state: it fades in and slides up from below into place (translateY(0)) via the --dur-ui token. Tab once on page load to reveal; activate to jump anchor to #main.

Sits at the very top of the page's <header>, as the first focusable element. Every page's <main> element must carry id="main" so the anchor resolves.

CSS

.ds-skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  top: 16px;          /* resting position — top-left */
  left: 16px;
  z-index: 100;
  padding: 12px 20px;
  background: var(--orange-500);
  color: var(--white);
  font-family: 'JetBrains Mono', monospace;
  font-size: 12px;
  font-weight: 600;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  text-decoration: none;
  border-radius: var(--r-control);
  opacity: 0;                  /* hidden: faded out + nudged down, non-interactive */
  transform: translateY(10px);
  pointer-events: none;
  transition: opacity var(--dur-ui) var(--ease-ui),
              transform var(--dur-ui) var(--ease-ui);
}
.ds-skip-link:focus,
.ds-skip-link:focus-visible {   /* fades in + slides up into place */
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
  pointer-events: auto;
  outline: 2px solid var(--orange-500);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
.ds-skip-link:hover { background: var(--orange-600); }   /* darken on hover */
/* Light-surface variant — dark-grey button */
.ds-skip-link--on-light { background: var(--grey-700); color: var(--white); }
.ds-skip-link--on-light:hover { background: var(--charcoal); }

Solutions

Four surfaces.
One platform underneath.

Different applications, the same loop. Whether the source is a screen, a live camera, a media archive, or a training corpus — the platform stays the same.

Agentic Perception

Give agents eyes, ears, and memory.

For AI agents, copilots, browser agents. Skill-first install across Claude Code, OpenAI, Cursor, n8n. OSS reference agents: pair-programmer, bloom, call.md.

Real-time Monitoring

Continuous perception for cameras, sensors, and live ops.

For ICU, industrial, drones, smart facilities. 1,000+ concurrent RTSP feeds. Custom CV indexes — bring your model. Sub-second alerts.

Programmable Media

Make video queryable, editable, and streamable by code.

For OTT, broadcasters, archives, AI editing. Search 2,500+ hours with playable evidence. AI clip factories, multi-language dubs, live event enrichment.

World Model Training Data

Prepare video data for the physical AI era.

For world model labs, robotics teams, autonomy companies. Petabyte-scale ingest with provenance. Quality scoring, scene segmentation, lab-grade reproducibility.

<section class="ds-section ds-section--light ds-solutions-sticky">

              <div class="ds-solutions-content" data-step="0">…</div>

              <div class="ds-solutions-content" data-step="2" inert>…</div>
              <div class="ds-solutions-content" data-step="3" inert>…</div>
            </div>

          </div>
